extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in political philosophy, public policy, and the relation of church and state
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative principles for composing or evaluating argumentative political essays—especially arguments about the proper role of government in religion—emphasizing argumentative rigor, testing general principles against particulars, and attention to practical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require strong proof for startling consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: “When the consequences of a doctrine are so startling, we may well require that its foundations shall be very solid.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a proposed principle implies surprising or sweeping outcomes (e.g., state control over religion), demand very full and accurate demonstration before accepting it. The essay uses the boldness of the doctrine as a reason to insist on stronger evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test abstract propositions by running over particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: “The moment that we examine these propositions closely, the moment that we bring them to the test by running over but a very few of the particulars which are included in them, we find them to be false and extravagant.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a purported general principle to concrete, varied examples (stage-coach companies, railway directors, banks, clubs, armies) to reveal unintended or absurd implications. Use concrete counterexamples to falsify overbroad claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming an overbroad major premise
rubrics_metrics.description: The author criticises Gladstone: he 'first resolves on his conclusion. He then makes a major of most comprehensive dimensions, and having satisfied himself that it contains his conclusion, never troubles himself about what else it may contain.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware the logical error of constructing an excessively large blanket premise that trivially contains the desired conclusion; check what else the premise entails and whether those entailments are reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate distinct ends (temporal duties vs. propagation of religion)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Now here are two great objects: one is the protection of the persons and estates of citizens from injury; the other is the propagation of religious truth. No two objects more entirely distinct can well be imagined.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating policy or institutional roles, explicitly distinguish different institutional ends. Fitness for secular/governance tasks does not imply fitness to serve theological missions—treat these as separate criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require empirical/probabilistic assessment of government efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay demands that before accepting that rulers ought to use power to promote religion we be 'bound to prove that those persons are likely to do more good than harm by so employing their power.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies that entrust institutions with moral or religious aims must be justified by showing, with reference to historical experience and realistic assessment, that they will probably produce net benefit rather than harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject coercion and material incentives as reliable means to produce sincere belief
rubrics_metrics.description: “An inquirer who has no wish except to know the truth is more likely to arrive at the truth than an inquirer who knows that, if he decides one way, he shall be rewarded, and that, if he decides the other way, he shall be punished.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using rewards, penalties, tests, or civil disabilities to enforce religious conformity tends to produce hypocrites, nominal conformists, and malcontents, not genuine conviction; thus coercive means are poor instruments for promoting truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for slippery slopes to persecution when making religious propagation a state end
rubrics_metrics.description: If the propagation of religious truth be a principal end of government, the logic of such a position leads to enforcement measures and potentially sanguinary persecution: 'But why not roast Dissenters at slow fires? ... For nothing can be clearer than that, if you punish at all, you ought to punish enough.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether endorsing a state's duty to propagate religion logically entails progressively harsher measures; check whether acceptable intermediate policies are coherent or whether the principle yields extreme, perverse outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value focused cooperation despite doctrinal disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is lawful and expedient for men to unite in an association for the promotion of a good object, though they may differ with respect to other objects of still higher importance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the social value in allowing people with differing wider beliefs to cooperate on single practical aims; do not require full doctrinal agreement as a precondition for joint public action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sceptical of arguments that rely on unreal 'perfect government' hypotheticals
rubrics_metrics.description: The author warns that arguing about what a perfect government would do is of limited use because 'there is not, and never has been, any such government in the world' and theories true only under such suppositions are of little practical value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing policy proposals, prefer arguments and evidence grounded in realistic institutional conditions rather than conclusions that hold only in idealized, unattainable circumstances.
